slides.label: Logic Makes Geometry Inspectable
slides.notes: Open by placing the chapter inside the course arc: Euclid's diagrams suggested a proof culture, but Chapter 2 asks what a proof is allowed to use. The deck turns statements about points and lines into objects that can be tested in models without confusing a drawing with a theorem.

slides.label: Route Through The Chapter
slides.notes: Use the route map as a contract for the lecture. Each arrow changes the representation of the same geometric claim: first as language, then as a predicate, then as a model check, then as an isomorphism question, and finally as a proof obligation.

slides.label: Incidence Is The Lean Vocabulary
slides.notes: Slow down here and deliberately remove metric habits. In incidence geometry, the primitive data are points, lines, and the lies-on relation. No length, angle, betweenness, or coordinate measurement is available unless a later axiom family or model adds it explicitly.

slides.label: Sentences Become Predicates
slides.notes: Translate a familiar geometric sentence into a testable predicate. Students should hear that the symbols are not decoration: they specify inputs, quantifiers, and a relation. This is the point where informal diagram reading becomes an auditable statement about a structure.

slides.label: Truth In A Model Is Not Yet Theoremhood
slides.notes: Emphasize the central distinction of the chapter. A sentence may be true in the model on the screen because that model has special features. A theorem must survive every model satisfying the stated assumptions, so one successful finite check is evidence, not final permission.

slides.label: Proof State Ledger
slides.notes: Present proof as disciplined bookkeeping rather than as a polished paragraph. The assumptions column records what is licensed, the rule column records the permitted move, and the conclusion column records only what follows from those entries. This prepares students to locate hidden assumptions.

slides.label: A Seven Point Projective Model
slides.notes: Introduce the Fano-style sample as a small world rather than as a picture of ordinary space. The slide highlights the sanity counts from the notebook: seven points, seven lines, three points on each line, and twenty-one total incidences. Those counts make the model easy to audit.

slides.label: Pair Search Replaces Visual Guessing
slides.notes: Explain how the predicate any two points determine a line becomes a finite search. The learner should inspect the pair arrows and the line labels, then notice that a computer check and a hand check share the same structure: enumerate pairs and locate a unique witness.

slides.label: Truth Tables As Model Diagnostics
slides.notes: Connect this slide to the notebook's truth-table lab. A diagnostic table does not prove a theorem by itself, but it shows which sentences separate candidate worlds. The most useful table is often the one that reveals exactly which assumption changed the truth value.

slides.label: Isomorphism Preserves The Incidence Table
slides.notes: Define isomorphism operationally as a relabeling that preserves the yes-or-no incidence relation. The visual shows the same table before and after a permutation, so the key question is not whether the drawing looks different but whether every lies-on fact is carried to another lies-on fact.

slides.label: Automorphisms Are Internal Symmetries
slides.notes: After isomorphism, name automorphisms as symmetries of a model with itself. The important teaching move is to separate visual symmetry from incidence symmetry. A redrawn model can look less symmetric while the underlying automorphism group still preserves the same incidence data.

slides.label: Projective Closure Removes Parallels
slides.notes: Use projective behavior as an incidence decision rather than as a perspective trick. When every pair of lines meets, the language has no exceptional parallel case. The line at infinity is a model device that turns parallel directions into ordinary incidence points.

slides.label: Affine Geometry Deletes One Line
slides.notes: Show the affine plane as a deliberate deletion from the projective picture. Removing one line and its points restores parallel classes in the remaining world. This makes parallelism look less like visual obviousness and more like a structural feature produced by the chosen model.

slides.label: Countermodels Expose Hidden Assumptions
slides.notes: Frame countermodels as diagnostic instruments. If two axiom packages both satisfy the stated incidence rules but disagree on a proposed conclusion, the conclusion was not licensed by those rules alone. The model is therefore doing logical work, not merely providing an example.

slides.label: Diagrams Suggest; Incidence Decides
slides.notes: Use this warning to discipline visual reasoning. A drawing may make a line appear curved, straight, long, short, or parallel, but incidence geometry only records which points lie on which lines. The safe question is always which visual feature is an invariant of the model.

slides.label: A Small Incidence Lab
slides.notes: Assign the lab as an active lecture moment. Students can choose any two points, find the line witnessing their incidence claim, and then try a relabeling. The exercise is intentionally finite so that theorem-like language remains tied to a checkable table.

slides.label: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter question. Logic and incidence geometry make non-Euclidean study possible because they teach students to track assumptions, models, and invariants separately. That habit will matter later when parallelism, order, congruence, and continuity are separated.
